newsitem.title: USA: Arizona jail going to the dogs - literally.
newsitem.headline: Arizona jail going to the dogs - literally.

text.p: An Arizona jail is going to the dogs -- and the sheriff in these parts wouldn't have it any other way.
Maricopa County Sheriff Joe Arpaio said he plans to turn to high-tech canine cops to give him extra pairs of eyes and ears at his "tent city" jail in southwest Phoenix.
Arpaio told Reuters on Friday that he would unleash four specially trained German Shepherd dogs equipped with miniature video cameras to help keep tabs on those residing at the canvas facility.

"Dogs are a man's best friend, everyone knows that," said Arpaio, who has a reputation for controversial programmes such as women chain gangs. "But they may not be an inmate's best friend after we're finished."
Plans call for the canine guards to patrol the grounds of the minimum- and medium-security jail, which houses about 800 male and female prisoners who are serving sentences of less than a year.
The dogs' cameras will record the goings-on at the jail and broadcast them back live to the guard tower, Arpaio said.
Authorities said the price tag is not cheap at $3,200 per dog, including training. Arpaio said he expects to spend another $10,000 for the camera equipment.
But sheriff's officials said they hope the new canine guards will enable them to even the odds a little in a place where only three officers at a time are on duty.

Capt. Dave Wilson, who oversees the tent facility, said the dogs also will be used to help prevent drugs and other contraband from being smuggled in and sniff it out if it gets through security. "It's probably our biggest problem," Wilson said. "We do what we can, but we can't be everywhere."
For example, Wilson said that on Wednesday a vehicle pulled alongside the security fence and a package was tossed into the compound for one of the detainees.

The package was a comprehensive store of contraband to be sold or traded. It included some pornographic magazines, a small quantity of marijuana and rolling papers and 29 packs of cigarettes. The cigarettes, like the other materials, are banned and go for as much as $20 a pack inside the jail.
